title: 3. Plasticity and Learning
intro: A cortical column learns from the stream of input it receives, with no labels and no backpropagated error. This section covers the local learning rules and the circuit mechanisms that make that possible.

blocks.text: Picture a fresh column as a sheet of neurons wired almost at random. A few hours of sensory input later, some neurons respond selectively to edges, others to particular sequences, and the population as a whole uses a sparse code in which every input activates a small, characteristic set of cells. Three ingredients produce that change. First, synapses change according to local signals — the activity of the two neurons they connect, and sometimes a third modulatory signal. Second, inhibition forces neurons to compete, so that they specialise on different inputs instead of all learning the same thing. Third, homeostatic mechanisms keep every neuron's activity in a useful range, so that none goes silent and none takes over.

The learning rules in this section are local: each synapse updates using only information available at that synapse. That is what makes them biologically plausible and what makes them attractive on neuromorphic hardware, where on-chip learning engines (Loihi's programmable learning rules, for example) can only see pre- and postsynaptic traces. The cost of locality is that nothing guarantees the network as a whole learns something useful — that guarantee has to come from the architecture: competition, sparsity and homeostasis.
Pages in this section, in learning order

items: Hebbian Learning — Hebb's postulate, the covariance form, Oja's rule and BCM. Why plain Hebbian learning is unstable and how normalisation or a sliding threshold fixes it.

Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity — the pair-based rule measured by Markram et al. (1997) and Bi & Poo (1998), its learning window, trace-based online implementation, and an interactive explorer of the window and of weight trajectories.
Homeostatic Plasticity — synaptic scaling, adaptive thresholds, intrinsic plasticity and HTM boosting: slow processes that keep fast learning from running away.

Inhibition and k-Winners-Take-All — how inhibitory interneurons create competition and sparsity, from balanced E/I networks to the k-WTA abstraction, with a spiking layer you can switch between no inhibition, E/I feedback and k-WTA.
Sparse Distributed Representations — the mathematics of sparse codes: capacity, overlap, robustness to noise, unions and false-match probabilities, with an interactive calculator.

blocks.text: Why this matters for building a column

Almost every working unsupervised SNN layer combines the same three parts. Diehl & Cook's (2015) STDP network for MNIST is a good reference point: excitatory neurons learn with STDP, a matching inhibitory population implements soft winner-take-all, and each excitatory neuron has an adaptive threshold that rises whenever it fires. Remove the inhibition and all neurons learn the same prototype; remove the adaptive threshold and a few neurons win every input. The HTM spatial pooler (section 4) has the same structure in non-spiking form: Hebbian permanence updates, k-winners-take-all inhibition, and boosting as homeostasis.

The output of such a layer is a sparse distributed representation. Understanding SDR mathematics tells you how large and how sparse your layers need to be: for example, with n = 2048 cells and w = 40 active, the chance that a random pattern is mistaken for a stored one at a match threshold of 20 shared cells is around 10⁻²⁶, which is why a dendritic segment can recognise a pattern from a sample of only a few of its active cells.

items: Local rules (Hebbian, STDP) learn correlations; on their own they are unstable and make every neuron learn the same thing.
Competition through inhibition (soft or hard k-WTA) makes neurons specialise and produces sparse codes.
Homeostasis acts on slower timescales (seconds to days in biology) and keeps every neuron useful; in models it is usually an adaptive threshold, synaptic normalisation or boosting.
Sparse distributed codes are high-capacity and noise-tolerant, and they let neurons recognise patterns by sub-sampling — the property HTM and Thousand Brains models build on.
When a learning layer misbehaves, check the balance among these three ingredients before tuning the learning rule itself.
